item.title: The Iran war looms large as BRICS leaders gather in New Delhi
item.description:
As diplomats prepare for the BRICS Summit in New Delhi this weekend, the Iran war is looming large.

India, which assumed the BRICS chairmanship in January, was already facing the difficult responsibility of securing consensus to achieve concrete movement on a variety of trade, economic, and financial objectives. Now, the U.S.-Israeli campaign against Iran has dramatically complicated this effort, throwing the global economy into uncertainty and dividing BRICS countries, including some that are actively participating on either side of the conflict.

The tensions within the bloc are far more significant than they were leading into last year’s summit in Brazil, which took place shortly after the 12-Day War against Iran. At that meeting, leaders condemned “the military strikes against the Islamic Republic of Iran since 13 June 2025, which constitute a violation of international law.” In addition, they called for an “immediate, permanent and unconditional ceasefire, and the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip.”

The situation in 2026 is more complicated. India — one of the five original BRICS members, alongside Brazil, Russia, China and South Africa — continues to strengthen its relationship with Israel just as the war in Iran exacerbates other BRICS members’ relationships with Tel Aviv. Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu just a few days before Israel and the United States attacked Iran in February 2026. As the Guardian notes, the visit marked a continuation of “India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East.”

Given such overtures to Israel, one may understand if the majority of BRICS countries are uncomfortable with India’s chairmanship during this year’s summit. This was not the case last year in Brazil.

Another aggravating factor is the fact that several BRICS members are now rival combatants. Iran, which joined the grouping in 2024, has damaged relations with many of its neighbors by attacking infrastructure and U.S. bases located on their territory. This includes the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, both of which are also BRICS members.

According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, “the UAE has been attacked by more Iranian projectiles than all other [Gulf Cooperation Council] states combined and incurred by far the greatest and most varied damage within the group.” As a result, the United Arab Emirates announced an indefinite trade embargo on Iran, saying “all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran have been halted until further notice.”

At the BRICS Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in May, the bloc released a comparatively weaker outcome document than that of the previous year, encouraging the international community “to continue supporting the Palestinian people in their pursuit of independence and sovereignty.” Moreover, the ministers were unable to produce a unified statement supporting Iran’s calls for “nations to condemn the U.S. and Israel over what they described as their unlawful aggression.” Therefore, we should expect that any final BRICS declaration will steer clear of any mention of the war in Iran.

Given these and other pre-existing divisions among BRICS members, the summit’s success will largely depend on whether India can achieve consensus on the economic agenda. Therefore, according to Asia One, it is important that India has centered its BRICS agenda on “institutional reforms that improve coordination while ensuring the bloc’s focus on development and cooperation rather than geopolitical rivalry.”

According to the BRICS 2026 website, Modi defines Delhi's objective for the summit as to redefine “BRICS as Building Resilience and Innovation for Cooperation and Sustainability.” The BRICS “Namaste” logo for India 2026 importantly symbolizes “collective strength and unity.” This important message is graphically reinforced through the petal colors which represent all BRICS member countries.

An example of BRICS cooperation and unity occurred during the BRICS Trade Ministers Meeting in Jaipur in August. As reported by India’s Nation Press, the ministers successfully finalized work on the BRICS Strategy for Economic Partnership 2030. This marks a significant achievement and now the plan will be referred for formal endorsement by the BRICS Leaders at next week’s summit. The strategy covers such issues as trade, investment, digital economy, and sustainable development.

More specifically, BRICS Pay will receive a tremendous amount of attention during the summit as a result of threats to global payments and supply chains sparked by the wars in Ukraine and Iran. The cross-border settlement platform, which launched earlier this year, is designed to complement rather than replace SWIFT and reduce dollar dependency. BRICS Pay continues to integrate sovereign payment systems, including China's CIPS, India's UPI, Brazil's Pix, and Russia's SPFS.

In addition, Reuters reported earlier this year that the Reserve Bank of India recommended to the government that a proposal to connect Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) be included in the agenda for the 2026 BRICS summit. If the recommendation is adopted BRICS will move forward with a proposal to link the digital currencies of BRICS members for the first time.

Trump has been sharply critical of any BRICS efforts to get around the U.S.-led financial system, which gives the U.S. extraordinary leverage over other countries through sanctions and other similar measures. "Any country aligning themselves with the Anti-American policies of BRICS, will be charged an ADDITIONAL 10% tariff,” he wrote on Truth Social last July, adding that there “will be no exceptions to this policy.”

More recently, Trump's Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, has increased the aggressive trade stance of the U.S. by issuing “Operation Economic Outcast.” The purpose of the sanctions plan is to escalate the economic pressure on Iran, while also alerting countries that cooperate with Iran that the U.S. could restrict access to the U.S. financial system if they continue doing business with Tehran.

Bessent’s policy reflects Washington’s frustration that the war in Iran has not achieved its aims. Instead, it has strengthened ties between some BRICS members and Iran, including Russia and China, which continue to provide crucial economic and political support to Iran’s efforts to withstand U.S. pressure.

Subsequently, China and Russia now support a greater profile for Iran in BRICS institutions at the upcoming summit, which Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend. Abdolnasser Hemmati, governor of the Central Bank of Iran, had indicated Iran would seek membership to BRICS Bank during the meeting in Delhi, according to CNBC.

It is clear India will have a difficult task as this year’s BRICS Summit host, presiding over a growing and increasingly divided group. One would expect India, contrary to other BRICS members, to make a concerted effort to assure any final declaration underscores that BRICS does not exist as an anti-Western bloc or seek to accelerate de-dollarization.

However, as a champion of multipolarity, economic sovereignty, and the Global South, India is positioned to overcome existing geopolitical divisions to successfully build a consensus among like-minded BRICS members. Ultimately, its success will require achieving cooperation on core BRICS initiatives related to the building of alternative structures for global economic growth, innovation, sustainability, and governance.

item.title: By shunning the Taliban, the world is hurting normal Afghans
item.description:
Kabul — Last month, when Aisha Wahab of California became the first Afghan-American elected to Congress, her victory was heralded as a sign that Afghans had truly made their mark in American society.

Afghan social media was inundated with messages of pride and celebration, Western-funded diaspora media outlets rushed out “who is Aisha Wahab” pieces, and even former President Hamid Karzai congratulated the 38-year-old on her victory.

But that celebration was short-lived.

During an appearance on Democracy Now after her election, Wahab said the United States “should pursue diplomacy” with Afghanistan, “regardless of which group is in power.”

Wahab acknowledged the severe limitations placed on women and girls under Taliban rule but said that, by exercising diplomacy with the Islamic Emirate government, the U.S. could possibly steer the Taliban “in the right direction when it comes to human rights, women’s rights and just civil rights across the board.”

That interview led to immediate condemnation. A week after her victory, many of the same Afghans who were cheering her on turned against Wahab, labeling her a Taliban apologist and even leaking private photos of her and her family to social media.

But here’s the thing: as much as the rest of the diaspora may hate to admit it, Wahab is correct. As an Afghan-American who has been living in Kabul since 2013, I have seen firsthand that the West’s efforts to punish the Taliban — seizing billions in Central Bank reserves, slashing foreign aid, closing embassies, cutting the nation’s banks off from the global financial system through financial restrictions — have greatly hurt the people, not the government.

It’s not just me who says this, though. In 2023, Karen Decker, then chargé d'affaires of the U.S. mission to Afghanistan, told me Washington needed to pursue a policy of “pragmatic engagement” with the Taliban. As she put it, “isolation is ruinous. It's ruinous for the Afghan people. It's ruinous for the region.”

The signs of that ruin are clear. At least 22 million Afghans, including 10.7 million women and girls, remain in need of humanitarian access. Since the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, that number has never been below 20 million, nearly half the population.

And the unwillingness to engage with the Taliban authorities has only added to the pressures faced by the organizations trying to address the malnutrition, poverty, and displacement affecting tens of millions of Afghans.

“Humanitarian actors have spent the last five years being the middlemen between the international community and the Taliban,” Samira Sayed-Rahman, an Afghan-Canadian humanitarian worker, told me last month in the lead-up to the fifth anniversary of the U.S. withdrawal. International organizations, she said, have been left with the onus of negotiating access, exemptions to edicts and bans, and the space to implement programs. Under normal circumstances, she said, all of that would fall to the donors themselves.

This was most clearly borne out in late 2022, when the Islamic Emirate banned Afghan women from working for NGOs, including the United Nations. It quickly became clear that negotiations were unavoidable, especially for smaller local organizations. Heads of local female-run organizations went to work to secure workarounds and exemptions while international organizations were in the middle of a shut down in protest.

Eventually, even the international organizations were left with no choice but to talk.

In the summer of 2023, Norwegian Refugee Council Secretary General Jan Egeland, confirmed his organization had “resumed most of our humanitarian operations in Kandahar as well as a number of other regions in Afghanistan.” Every other NGO leader I spoke to at the time, including Afghan women who ran smaller local organizations, said they chose to keep their workarounds quiet, worried the publicity would get the exemptions pulled.

Those exemptions, along with the continued operation of unofficial schools for girls beyond the sixth grade, prove that though their leader may be stubborn and unmoving, there are more moderate forces within the Taliban.

Pushing organizations to negotiate directly with the government, rather than leaving that to the donors, Sayed-Rahman added, isn’t a mere inconvenience. It can be dangerous, especially for Afghan nationals. It also asks apolitical organizations that were meant to hand out food, build schools, and run clinics to take on issues like girls’ access to education, women’s right to work, and educational curricula. The recent global aid cuts, including the 2025 gutting of USAID, have only made the situation more dire in Afghanistan, Flora Alexander, Executive Director of IRC UK, said after a week-long visit to the country.

“There are currently multiple converging and overlapping crises” in Afghanistan, Alexander said, citing issues around climate change, the return of five million Afghans from Iran and Pakistan, and the continued challenges to education for women and girls.

Alexander said a visit to a medical center in the eastern province of Nangarhar illustrated how important it is for Western countries to find ways to provide assistance to Afghanistan.

“This used to be a full-service primary health facility covering malnutrition, mental health, communicable and non-communicable diseases. Today, it’s just reproductive health and family planning,” she said of the Khogyani district clinic.

Most jarring for Alexander was the fact that it would only cost about $5,000 a month to restore the clinic to its former status.

Alexander said there is an ongoing debate over how to address humanitarian needs without formally recognizing the government. This philosophical debate “is used as justification by some countries to not engage in humanitarian aid,” she said.

However, she added, what these countries must realize is that providing assistance to health programs, for instance, is “a proven way of meeting health needs and ensuring that women can work and girls can continue to develop,” despite the Islamic Emirate’s restrictions.

Further, the Taliban does want a relationship with the United States. This was made clear by both George W. Bush’s ambassador to Afghanistan and the Islamic Emirate’s own Minister of Foreign Affairs, Amir Khan Muttaqi, who told the Financial Times that Washington is welcome to invest in Afghanistan $1 trillion in mineral assets.

Most importantly, Muttaqi said sanctions and other restrictions on the Taliban leadership “did not achieve their intended objectives.”

The biggest objection to engagement with the Islamic Emirate remains the serious human rights concerns in the country. Washington cited these, along with the charge that the Islamic Emirate is “a global terrorist organization” in their rebuke of Muttaqi’s offer, saying investment in mining would only enable the Taliban’s “horrific treatment” of the Afghan people.

But the reality is that sanctions and diplomatic shunning have done little to disempower or dissuade the Taliban. Having seen the effects of international isolation with my own eyes, one thing has become clear: punishing the government has not worked. It has punished everyone but the government.

item.title: Will the UN vote to sustain Haiti’s Gang Suppression Force?
item.description:
Will the UN vote to sustain Haiti’s Gang Suppression Force? Expert comment jon.wallace 10 September 2026

Sustaining the force is essential. But so too are funding commitments to restore the health and education services Haitians desperately need.

On 30 September the UN Security Council will vote on renewing the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) for Haiti. 

Now is not the time to pull the plug on GSF and its security effort. If anything, the Security Council vote should be an opportunity to swiftly renew the force and then confront an additional uncomfortable issue: How can development assistance be mobilized for Haiti, among a fractured international donor community?

‘Haitian-led’

After the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse, a mantra took hold among diplomats that any solution to the country’s spiral of chaos and crime needed to be ‘Haitian-led’. It’s a nice phrase, intended to reassure sceptics that a solution would not be imposed on Haiti. 

But how are Haitians supposed to lead?

Haiti hasn’t had an election since 2016. There is no elected government at any level – local, departmental, parliamentary or presidential. Political parties are in disarray. Many are still controlled by the same distrusted leaders that have dominated Haitian politics for decades. 

Indeed, according to a Chatham House-QQ survey, more than 75 per cent of Haitians don’t trust their political leadership. And civil society remains fragmented, weak and often distant from political power – despite years of international development support. 

That leaves the international community with continued responsibility to help get Haiti back on its feet. And that means doing much more than funding the vital GSF.

Respondents to the Chatham House-QQ survey identified education and healthcare as priorities in re-establishing security: 69.1 per cent and 67.3 per cent respectively. Development assistance will be needed to deliver these basic services. But where will it come from? 

Fragile progress

Chatham House’s survey was conducted in May 2026. That was a month after the first GSF contingent of 400 Chadian troops arrived in Haiti and following operations by the Haitian National Police (HNP) against the gangs that control almost all of Port-au-Prince. An estimated 1,300 gang leaders and members were killed in those operations.  Those efforts were assisted by divisions within the coalition of gangs that had come to dominate parts of Haiti and its economy.  

At the time of the survey, a slight majority of Haitians (50.7 per cent) were starting to believe that their communities had become safer. But support for the GSF was mixed: 49.5 per cent of voting age respondents said they approved or strongly approved of the multinational force. 

Related work

What Haitians want from the next phase of UN and international support

Unsurprisingly, that support was greater among Haitians living on the front lines of the insecurity, in or close to gang-controlled areas, where more than 67 per cent approved or strongly approved. 58.4 per cent of Haitians between the ages of 18 and 29 – a key demographic for Haiti’s recovery and future – also showed strong support for the GSF. 

Yet 54.2 per cent of Haitians polled don’t believe the GSF can accomplish its mission. 

At best, Haitians are modestly optimistic. But the window of opportunity to channel even this limited support may close quickly. The Security Council must act to build on what fragile progress has been made. 

The development need 

The importance of effectively addressing Haiti’s failed state and humanitarian disaster goes beyond Haiti and the security risks it presents to the Caribbean. Much is at stake for the United Nations, and the future of international cooperation.

The GSF resolution of 2025 was a rare victory for the UN after past resolutions had been vetoed by China and Russia. And it sets a model for how the international community, including many countries from the Global South, can still collaborate to respond to humanitarian tragedies.  

Kenya and Chad contributed troops. Canada committed funding and was instrumental in pushing the GSF approval over the line last year. Germany, Qatar and the US have also contributed funding. Mexico, Colombia, El Salvador, Jamaica and Brazil have made in-kind contributions through training, materiel and advisors. 

The Haiti resolution demonstrates that the international community can come together, even in this semi-ad hoc fashion, to respond to humanitarian crises – even when faith in the international system is waning. The courageous work of UN officials and diplomats posted in Haiti coordinating this effort is a testament to the enduring belief in global institutions and the principles under which they were founded. 

But the work is only beginning. If the GSF can establish itself, the next phase will bring new challenges, mainly related to development. Without the US Agency for International Development (USAID), who will step up to coordinate the next essential stage of Haiti’s recovery? The US now lacks the resources, commitment and moral authority to convene a donors’ conference and mobilize resources and commitments for Haitians’ needs. Are solutions still possible without the might of the US to drive them?

Who will step up? 

When the Security Council gathers to approve the renewal of the GSF, the hope is that their discussion will progress beyond security to the broader challenges of how to restore a shattered and brutalized country. Reaching agreement on a security force is a beginning only. New commitments must be made to invest in Haiti’s education, healthcare, and economic future.

The US’s commitment to focus on security and ‘gang suppression’ first was necessary. And its pushing through of a Security Council resolution that would focus on protecting Haitians was both successful and laudable. 

But there is now a need to work in parallel on social and economic development and the rebuilding of Haiti’s battered physical and institutional infrastructure. That will take funding by a broad group of donors and agreement on where and how to invest to the best effect.  

It will also require more than the kind of concessional loans normally offered by development banks. Haiti’s interim government is too broken to commit to such debts. Instead, those banks should work with supportive governments to develop an incentive-based, conditional partnership with the interim government – or its successor. That would involve agreeing to release funds when Haiti’s government reaches benchmarks in security, fiscal, healthcare, education and macroeconomic reform.

The US Development Finance Corporation (DFC) must also play a key role. The well-bank-rolled DFC can provide investor insurance and concessionary loans to encourage private investors to fill the gaps left by the elimination of USAID. Frankly, they will probably do it better than USAID because of their focus on investment, trade and results. 

However, that will require a more concentrated effort by the DFC to focus on Haiti. The DFC’s mandate to ‘mobilize private capital to advance US foreign policy’ can equally apply to other donors, including government development agencies, private foundations and multilateral development banks. 

Rebuilding Haiti and protecting the security of Haitians by battling gangs is not just a US foreign policy interest. Haiti has already become a vector for gun smuggling, narcotics trafficking and other illicit activities. Further state collapse would only bring greater insecurity, and not only to its neighbours in the Caribbean (including UK Commonwealth countries), Mexico and the US. The longer the crisis goes on the greater the risk that Haiti becomes a stateless hub for transnational crime – affecting every country with an Atlantic coast.

Lieut. Gen. (Ret.) H.R. McMaster commanded in Afghanistan and Iraq, oversaw training and modernization for the US Army’s infantry, armor, and cavalry force, and was an assistant professor of history at the US Military Academy. Hear one of America’s leading security and military thinkers talk about China, Europe, Iran, and the future of the US in an increasingly contested world.

The United States faces mounting challenges as strategic competition intensifies, and conflicts reshape the international order. War with Iran, ongoing Russian aggression against Ukraine, rising tensions with China and fraying relationships with allies are changing Washington’s approach to global leadership. These developments raise fundamental questions about America’s role as a security guarantor, and the future of the transatlantic relationship.

General McMaster will discuss:

  • What are the most significant national security challenges facing the United States?
  • How should Washington respond to the rise of China?
  • What is the future of the transatlantic relationship and US–Europe cooperation?
  • How can the United States strengthen deterrence while managing global commitments?
  • What role should America play as a guarantor of international security?
  • How is geopolitical competition reshaping the international order?

item.title: Trump’s comments on the Falkland Islands reflect a fractured US-UK relationship
item.description:
President suggested US might not help UK if Argentina tried to seize Falklands – a new low for UK-US ‘special relationship’

Last week, Donald Trump suggested in an interview with the British TV channel GB News that he might not help the UK if Argentina tried again to seize the Falkland Islands. It was a new low for UK-US relations.

The “special relationship” (Winston Churchill’s phrase) was never perfect, but the UK helped the US on countless occasions, from Korea to Iraq to Afghanistan. The US often stood by the UK as well – although not during the Suez Crisis of 1956, but Ronald Reagan’s government provided significant intelligence and logistics support to Britain during the dust-up over the Falklands in 1982. That relationship is fading fast.

item.title: The UK’s sanctions on Israeli settlements are a great victory – but must be only the beginning | Em Hilton
item.description:
The change in policy is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement. But what comes next?

The announcement on Tuesday by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, of an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, as well as a comprehensive sanctions regime, is a hard-won victory for the Palestine solidarity movement.

This is not simply a change of heart by the government: it is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement, who have consistently held the government’s feet to the fire over its complicity in the atrocities being committed in Gaza and the West Bank. Miliband’s announcement shows us what organised and persistent campaigning can achieve, and inspires confidence that movements can force political change.

Em Hilton is a Jewish writer and organiser. She is the co-founder of Na’amod: UK Jews Against Israeli Occupation, and the policy director at Diaspora Alliance
